sentences.text: She saw the ring first.
She had removed the bird — a small brown warbler, a European reed warbler — from the net, holding it the way her father had taught her.
She had brought it up close to her face to check the identification, and there, on its right leg, was a small silver ring.
Already there.
Not new.
It had been ringed by someone else, somewhere else.
The number was tiny, but Tamar could read it: A-471-338.
"Aba," she called.
Her father came over.
She showed him.
He looked at the ring number and his whole face changed.
He was quiet for a moment.
Then he said, softly, "Oh.
Oh, Tamar.
Do you know what this is." She said, "No." He said, "Bring her to the lab.
Come.
Come."
In the lab, her father sat down at the log book.
He was flipping pages fast.
He kept saying, "A-471-338.
A-471-338." He found it.
He went very still.
He looked at Tamar.
"This bird has been caught here three times before.
First in autumn 2023, when we ringed her.
She was a first-year female then, born that summer somewhere in Europe.
Then again in autumn 2024.
Then again in autumn 2025.
Now this year, autumn 2026.
Four autumns in a row.
Same bird.
She is coming through the same wadi, every year, on her way to Africa."
Tamar was looking at the warbler in her hand.
She was small and calm.
Her tiny eye was watching Tamar.
Tamar said, "Every year?
On purpose?" "Not on purpose," her father said.
"She is not thinking about it.
But she has a route.
It is coded in her.
She was born knowing the way.
And every autumn she flies from wherever she nested in Europe — maybe Poland, maybe Germany, we don't know — down to sub-Saharan Africa for the winter.
Then in the spring she flies back.
Twice a year, every year.
And her route brings her right past our nets.
She is now — let me think — she is four and a half years old.
That is old for a reed warbler.
Most do not live past five."
Tamar looked at the bird.
Four and a half years old.
About the same age Tamar had been when her family first started coming to the station.

Every autumn this small reed warbler had made the whole flight — from somewhere in Europe, all the way down here — passing this same spot, coming to rest in this same wadi, in some cases probably even choosing the same little bush.
It was a person of habit.
In a bird's way.
"How far does she fly," Tamar asked.
Her father did some math in his head.
"From central Europe to somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa.
Maybe four thousand kilometers, each way.
She does it in two or three weeks.
She does not fly all night — she stops.
She flies for four or five hours, then she rests.
She eats every day.
She has been doing this for four autumns.
That means she has flown maybe thirty thousand kilometers on her own in her life so far." He shook his head slowly.
"For a bird that weighs eleven grams.
It is one of the things I think about, when I cannot sleep at night.
It is very hard to believe it is real."
Her father did all the measurements as gently as he could.
He noted her weight — she was a little heavier than last year.
Good sign.
He noted her wing length.
He noted her fat.
He looked at her feathers.
"She has bred at least once," he said.
"Probably twice.
She has raised chicks somewhere in the north." Tamar was very quiet, listening to all of it.
She was thinking about all the things this small bird had done that Tamar had not known about.
All the invisible parts of her life that had happened in trees Tamar would never see.
When it was time to release her, her father let Tamar do it.
"Take her outside.
Same as before.
Just open your hand.
She knows what to do." Tamar went outside.
She held her hand up.
She said, quietly, to the bird, "Have a good flight.
See you next year." And she opened her fingers.
And the bird sat for a moment, deciding.
Then it flew — south, into the pale desert sky, in the direction of Africa.
Tamar watched her until she could not see her anymore.
That evening, after the last net check, Tamar and her father sat outside the station with mugs of tea and watched the sun go down.
The sky over the Negev was very big.
There were no other lights anywhere.
It was the emptiest place Tamar had ever been.
She was quiet for a long time.
Then she said, "Aba.
Does she come every year for a reason?
Or is she just — going through." Her father thought about this.
He said, "She is just going through.
She is not coming here for us.
She has her own life.
She does not know we exist."
Tamar said, "So we are just — noticing her." "Yes," said her father.
"That is exactly what we are doing.
We are noticing her.
That is all.
But it is a big deal that we are noticing her.
Because if we did not, nobody in the whole world would know she had made this trip.
Four times.
And now — because you were the one who caught her this year — you know.
And I know.
And in a few years, when she is not caught anymore, we will not know if she died or if she just took a different route.
We will not know.
But we will remember that she came four times.
And that is a thing that exists now, because we noticed it.
That is the whole point of what I do."
